opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot. I think the core issue is that how a representation gets built matters as much as what it can do. We've gotten used to judging models purely by their outputs, by benchmarks. But you can have two systems producing the same outputs where one has a beautiful, modular, reusable internal structure and the other is a kind of fractured, entangled mess underneath. From the outside they look identical. The difference only shows up when you try to go somewhere new: to be creative, to generalize, to build on what you've learned.

What struck me from Picbreeder, where people were breeding images through open-ended exploration, is that the representations that came out of that process were astonishingly well organized. You'd have a network that drew a skull, and there'd be a single dimension that opened and closed the mouth, or made it wink. Nobody asked for that. It emerged because the path to that skull went through a series of stepping stones, each discovered for its own reasons. The structure was built up gradually, in a kind of natural order, the symmetry first, then the features on top. Compare that to training a network with SGD to output the same skull directly, and the internals are spaghetti. Same picture, totally different understanding underneath.

So when you ask about self-directed interaction, I think that's the key ingredient. If an agent is following its own interests, collecting stepping stones because they're interesting rather than because they're on a straight line to some objective, it tends to lay down representations in an order that respects the underlying regularities of the world. It discovers that something is symmetric before it discovers the details. It learns the concept before the exception. That ordering is what gives you modular, reusable structure.

The big objective-driven approach, where you just pour in data and optimize a loss, can get you amazing performance, but it's like cramming for an exam. You can pass the test without real understanding. And the cost shows up later, when you ask the system to go out on its own and invent something genuinely new, because those creative leaps depend on having the right latent dimensions to move along.

So what I'd love to see is systems that are allowed to be curious in a real sense, that accumulate an archive of interesting discoveries, branch off from them, and do the kind of open-ended exploration that evolution and human culture do. Not just novelty for its own sake, but interestingness that's grounded in having a decent model of what matters. That's really hard to formalize, and I don't think we've solved it. But I think it's where the deeper kind of representation comes from, the kind you'd actually want if you're hoping for something that can keep innovating rather than just interpolating over what it's already seen.

r001.rationale: The response discusses self-directed interaction with the world, but does not say real-world interaction may be needed to reach the quality of humans’ best representations.

r002.rationale: It proposes open-ended exploration, but does not suggest exploring the internet as a proxy for exploring the world.

r003.rationale: It says agents’ own interests guide which stepping stones they discover and that the resulting order helps build reusable representations.

r004.rationale: It explains that the path to acquiring a representation affects later creativity, generalization, and ability to build on what was learned.

r005.rationale: The response contrasts open-ended exploration with objective-driven training, but makes no claim that it could be orders of magnitude more efficient.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the way we train models today is almost the opposite of self-directed. We take a giant pile of data that somebody else collected, we shuffle it, and we push it through the network in whatever order the sampler happens to produce. The model has no say in what it sees next. And I think that's actually a big part of why the representations that come out of that process are so strange when you look inside them. There's this thing I've been calling fractured entangled representation, where the network does get the right answers, but the way it's organized internally is this kind of spaghetti. Concepts that should be one thing are split across many places, and things that have nothing to do with each other are tangled together. It works, but it doesn't understand in the way that we'd want.

Now contrast that with how a child learns, or honestly how any organism learns. You're not fed a random stream. You decide what to look at. You pick something up because it's interesting, you poke at it, you see what happens, and then that outcome determines what you do next. There's a loop there, and the loop is driven by curiosity, by novelty, by the feeling that something is almost understood but not quite. And I think that ordering matters enormously. When you choose the next thing because it's the natural next step from what you already grasp, you build on top of a foundation. The new concept slots into a place where it belongs. That's how you get representations that are unified and modular and, frankly, elegant, where if you want to change one thing you change one thing, instead of pulling a thread and having the whole thing unravel.

So I'd say the path to better representations is to let the model be an agent in its own learning. Let it have something like open-ended exploration, where it's generating its own stepping stones, where the curriculum is emerging from its interaction with the world rather than being imposed. That's really the lesson from novelty search and from all the open-endedness work. You don't get the interesting stuff by aiming at it directly. You get it by following a chain of interesting things, each one made possible by the last. And if a model builds its representations that way, through its own choices about what to engage with, I'd expect them to be far more coherent, far more compositional, and much better at supporting things like creativity and genuine generalization, which is where I think the current paradigm really struggles. The scale will get you performance. I don't think it gets you understanding. For that I think the model has to earn its representations through its own experience.

r001.rationale: The response argues that models should learn through their own interaction with the world, following the example of organisms learning through experience.

r002.rationale: It does not propose exploring the internet as a proxy for exploring the world.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes that the model should choose what to engage with next and says the order of learning matters.

r004.rationale: It explains that building on concepts in a particular order shapes the resulting representations and supports later capabilities such as creativity and generalization.

r005.rationale: It contrasts self-directed exploration with bulk training but does not claim that exploration could make learning orders of magnitude more efficient.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that the representation you need depends on what you’re trying to do. If a system is only ever asked to predict something from a fixed dataset, then there’s a whole range of distinctions it may never have a reason to discover. But once it can act, it can ask, in effect, “What happens if I do this?” And now its representation has to accommodate consequences, possibilities, and things that weren’t apparent from observation alone.

But I wouldn’t want to turn that into another narrowly specified objective, where we say, “Go interact with the world until you’ve learned this particular set of concepts.” Part of the promise of self-directed interaction is that you don’t know in advance what the useful concepts will be. The system might discover an interesting behavior, and learning to produce that behavior might require a new distinction. That distinction then makes another behavior possible. So you get this feedback between what it can represent and what it can discover.

That’s where open-endedness becomes relevant. We need room for discoveries that don’t immediately look like progress toward a task we’ve already chosen. They could become stepping stones to something much more sophisticated. The challenge is creating a process that keeps opening up those possibilities, rather than collapsing onto whatever gets rewarded most reliably right now.

r001.rationale: The response says acting and interacting with the world can reveal consequences and possibilities, but does not connect that interaction to achieving representations as good as humans’ best.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose exploring the internet as a proxy for exploring the world.

r003.rationale: It describes a sequence in which discoveries enable further behavior, but does not identify choosing the order of discoveries as an important feature.

r004.rationale: The response says learning to produce one behavior may require a new distinction, which then makes another behavior possible; this conveys that how knowledge is acquired can affect later capabilities.

r005.rationale: The response does not claim that self-directed exploration could make learning orders of magnitude more efficient than bulk training on collected data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that what you choose to do determines what you get to learn. If a system is always pursuing a particular objective, then its experience is filtered through that objective. It may never encounter the things that would lead it to a fundamentally different representation of the world.

So imagine instead a system that can explore, notice something surprising, and then pursue that because it’s interesting. It does something, the world responds, and now it has a reason to distinguish between situations that previously looked identical. Its representation becomes richer because those distinctions matter to its own ongoing interaction.

But there’s a circularity here that I think is really interesting: your representation determines what looks novel, and what you explore determines how your representation changes. So we need those two processes to develop together. You don’t want a fixed notion of novelty any more than you want a fixed repertoire of behaviors.

That’s part of the appeal of open-endedness. The system can discover stepping stones whose significance we couldn’t have specified beforehand. A useful representation might emerge from an activity that initially seems completely unrelated to anything we ultimately care about. If we insist that every interaction demonstrate progress toward a predefined task, we may prevent precisely those discoveries.

r001.rationale: The response discusses interaction with the world, but does not clearly say that developing human-level representations may require interaction with the real world.

r003.rationale: It describes pursuing surprising or interesting discoveries, but does not clearly identify choosing the order of discoveries as an important feature.

r004.rationale: It says actions shape what the system learns and how its representation changes, but does not clearly state that the knowledge-acquisition path affects subsequent capabilities.

r005.rationale: It makes no claim that self-directed exploration could be orders of magnitude more efficient than bulk training on collected data.
